job: JOB 1: Fascia sign PERMIT OFFICE (clean quartz band, gold lettering pixels)
why: The gold lettering pixels on the quartz fascia band move the sign toward the concept's PERMIT OFFICE text and add a crafted accent, though the scattered gold blocks do not yet form legible letters and read slightly as noise.

job: JOB 2: Cyan end caps of the fascia sign
why: The cyan end caps now wrap down past the fascia as short vertical returns on both sides, echoing the concept's cyan edge trim on the Permit Office sign, though the added blocks are small and slightly stark in the street view.

job: JOB 3: Plaque INSPECTORATE (stone tablet, dark lettering)
why: The tablet's raised carved-square panels were replaced with flat pale stone plus dark blocks and a wood post cutting into the sign band, so it looks patchy and broken rather than a legible INSPECTORATE plaque with lettering.

job: JOB 4: Square-boss end blocks of plaque and pier feet
why: The square-boss end blocks add carved-block terminals to the plaque ends and pier feet, echoing the concept's boxed bosses, with no silhouette or colour disruption, though the effect is small.

job: JOB 5: Gold cross emblem in the pediment
why: The gold cross in the pediment matches the concept's gold emblem, gives the plain triangular gable a focal point, and reads as a deliberate ornament, though it is a chunky, slightly irregular cross with a lighter-shaded notch rather than a crisp, thin one.

job: JOB 6: Stepped raking cornice of the pediment
why: The change adds small stepped corner blocks at the raking cornice ends of the pediment, giving the gable a slightly more crafted, framed edge that echoes the concept's stepped cornice, though the effect is subtle and the silhouette is otherwise unchanged.

job: JOB 7: Roof-corner and pediment-foot finials
why: The thin stone rods floating at the roof corners and pediment feet read as detached antennae (some hover in air off the roof edge in the elevation), adding clutter and a broken silhouette rather than the stepped, grounded finials in the concept.

job: JOB 9: Hanging lanterns on the upper corner piers
why: Small dark lanterns now hang from the upper corner piers, echoing the concept's corner lanterns with a bit of added depth and warm detail, though they are tiny and subtle at this scale and do not disturb the silhouette.

job: JOB 10: Ground-floor corner lamp-bracket arms
why: A small dark bracket arm with a hanging lantern now sits at the ground-floor corner, matching the concept's corner lamp brackets without breaking the silhouette, though it is tiny and only slightly warm.

job: JOB 11: Teal banners at the corners
why: The teal banners the job added at the corners are not visible in the front or front-left close-ups; the only change is a pair of light tan blocks on the dark door-frame pillar, which neither matches the teal banners in the concept nor harms the silhouette.

job: JOB 12: Copper downpipes beside the corner banners
why: The change adds a couple of small tan/terracotta blocks on the white pier faces at window height that read as stray patches rather than copper downpipes (no vertical run, wrong tone, barely visible), so it neither helps nor noticeably harms the facade.

job: JOB 13: Wall lanterns on the ground-floor piers
why: Two small lanterns now hang on the ground-floor piers beside the door, close to the concept's wall lanterns, but they are tiny and sit on a thin dark chain stub. They also look slightly off-pier in the front elevation, so they add a little detail without clearly improving or harming the build.

job: JOB 14: Hanging lanterns inside the arches
why: Small lanterns on chains now hang inside the arches and over the door, matching the concept's hanging lanterns and adding warm detail and depth without clutter or silhouette damage.

job: JOB 15: Stepped corbelled arches over the shopfront bays
why: The stepped corbelled arches are only faintly visible as slight stair-step notches in the pale stone above the bays, so the shopfront reads almost the same as before with no broken silhouette or wrong colour, but also little of the concept's arch profile.

job: JOB 16: Shopfront mullion grid
why: The mullion grid adds only faint, barely visible light-blue lines on the shopfront glass, so it moves slightly toward the concept's paned windows but doesn't change the silhouette or read clearly as a crafted improvement.

job: JOB 17: Double door with transom
why: The door is now a clean double door with a slightly narrower, framed transom under the lantern, but the change is tiny and barely shifts the overall read versus the concept's detailed double door.

job: JOB 18: Entrance steps nosed with stairs
why: the job changed no visible pixels in any view

job: JOB 19: Potted shrubs and topiary
why: the job changed no visible pixels in any view

job: JOB 20: Stone planter ledges before the shop windows
why: The planter ledges add only a thin pale-grey sill strip under the windows, with barely perceptible change in the street view and a small, flat addition in the front-left view, so it neither clearly improves nor harms the build.

job: JOB 21: Filing cabinet with scattered papers
why: The small barrel-like cabinet and white paper scraps on the dark plinth echo the concept's filing cabinet with scattered papers by the steps, adding a believable low-key detail without disturbing the silhouette or clashing in colour.

job: JOB 22: Interior furnishings
why: the job changed no visible pixels in any view

job: JOB 23: Plinth / base course
why: The after view adds a stepped, wider dark-stone plinth that grounds the building and matches the concept's base course, with only minor edges looking slightly blocky.

job: JOB 24: Paving apron
why: The only visible change is one pale, weathered-looking block inserted at the paving apron's edge, which adds slight texture variation but is too small to read as meaningful detail and its light tone is slightly off against the dark stone.

job: JOB 25: Moss and cracked weathering
why: The before and after renders look nearly identical at this scale, with only faint moss-green flecks on the plinth and base, so the weathering is too subtle to improve the build and too small to harm it.

job: JOB 26: Upper-storey window frames with transom bars
why: The upper-storey windows gain dark transom bars with timber mullions that add frame depth and read closer to the concept's multi-pane sash windows, though the dark gaps are slightly heavy and the effect is subtle at this scale.

job: JOB 27: Dark pilasters flanking the upper windows
why: The dark pilasters beside the upper windows are only faintly visible in the before/after crops and barely change the facade, and they add no clear depth or contrast toward the concept's dark framing.

job: JOB 28: Window hoods
why: The projecting stone hoods over the upper-storey windows add a lintel profile and depth that echo the concept's window surrounds, with no colour clash or silhouette break, though the effect is modest.

job: JOB 29: Stone window sills with corbels
why: The added stone sill slabs with corbel blocks under the upper-storey windows give the façade the projecting, layered window profile that the concept shows, and they sit in matching stone without breaking the silhouette.

job: JOB 30: Window boxes with flowers
why: Small flower boxes now sit under the upper-storey windows and match the concept's sill planters, adding a bit of life and depth without cluttering the facade or changing the silhouette, though the effect is subtle at this scale.

job: JOB 31: Louvred shutters
why: The shutters replace the glazed windows with a black void flanked by thin wood slats, so the windows lose their glass panes and mullions and read as empty dark holes, and the concept shows louvred shutters on only one upper window, not on every window.

job: JOB 32: Timber piers with bracket caps
why: The tan timber piers gain small bracket caps and stripe detailing at the top of the corner piers, echoing the concept's bracketed timber posts, with no colour clash or silhouette damage, though the change is subtle.

job: JOB 33: Slim mossy downpipe strips
why: The slim mossy strips are faintly visible as dark-green vertical lines beside the upper-storey window piers, but they're subtle and barely change the read of the facade, neither adding clear craft nor causing clutter.

job: JOB 34: Dentil row under the eave
why: the job changed no visible pixels in any view

job: JOB 35: Overhanging stone cornice
why: The cornice adds a thin horizontal line and small projecting ledges at the eaves and above the centre bay, but it is barely visible at this scale, and the stray protruding stubs at the sides read slightly as clutter rather than a true overhanging cornice profile.

job: JOB 36: Corner eave brackets
why: The change adds a few barely visible brown bracket blocks at the corner eave that blend into the existing timber and don't visibly alter the silhouette or finish.

job: JOB 37: Belt course between storeys
why: A continuous pale-stone belt course now separates the ground-floor arcade from the timber upper storey on both views, adding the horizontal banding and depth the concept has, without breaking the silhouette.

job: JOB 38: Side-return arcade posts
why: The arcade posts in the side-return change from a lighter brown brick-like texture to a darker, flatter dark-oak tone, which is a subtle recolour with no new profile or depth and little visible effect at this scale.

job: JOB 39: Roof edge coping
why: The roof edge coping adds only a faint light-grey cap line along the eaves, which is barely visible and does not noticeably change the silhouette or the craft level, though it is not harmful either.

job: JOB 40: Chimney with copper cap
why: The change adds a tall stone-brick chimney stack with a copper cap, which reads as a believable chimney and matches the concept's small chimney stacks on the roofline, replacing the earlier flat copper slab sitting on the roof. The copper cap is slightly boxy and the stack is a bit tall, but the form and materials are an improvement.
